title: Grateful Dead Live at Fillmore West on 1970-02-05
lineage: SBD MR > C > D > CD + AUD low-gen

ai_review.summary: Matrix source with generally good soundboard quality (some muddy audience bits) captures a smoking Feb 5 1970 show highlighted by a monster Mason's Children and fiery Eleven‑Caution sequence.
ai_review.review: The recording is a hybrid of sound‑board and audience sources; the later portion sounds crystal clear while the opening tracks are noticeably lo‑fi, with occasional bass‑low mix and treble‑bright issues. Musically the performance shines – Mason’s Children is repeatedly called the best on tape, The Eleven rolls into a classic Caution jam, and the NFA→Cumberland transition is praised by several listeners. Overall fans are enthusiastic despite the imperfect audio.

ai_rating.rationale: Most reviewers (≈80 %) give 4‑5 stars and highlight standout performances; recording issues are noted but limited to early audience tracks, so the weighted average of show (≈4.6) and recording (≈3.8) yields ~4.4.

recording_quality.technical_notes: Later half is crystal‑clear soundboard; first four tracks are lo‑fi audience with dead spots, bass a bit low and occasional treble harshness. Some reviewers note pitch/speed inconsistencies in AUD copies.

show_quality.setlist_flow: Set builds strong momentum from Mason's Children into a high‑energy Eleven → Caution sequence, with the NFA→Cumberland segue praised; missing China>Rider fragment noted but does not detract from overall flow.

band_member_comments.Jerry: Several reviewers note his adventurous jams (e.g., New Speedway Boogie in Big Boss Man) and a rare pedal‑steel cameo, adding extra excitement.
band_member_comments.Phil: His bass/lead work shines on Caution and the jam transitions; one reviewer calls his riff “insistent” and vital to the flow.
band_member_comments.Keys: Pigpen’s organ appears on The Eleven, an unusual but emotionally resonant contribution for this era.
band_member_comments.Drums: The drum sound is repeatedly praised – described as popping, crunchy, and bright; many cite the Bear‑mix style of the period.
